# Objective

The `dosefitr` package provides tools for fitting curves to data. This vignette walks through the main functionality of setting bounds on individual curve parameters.

```{r echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(dosefitr)
```

# Constraining curve parameters

By default, `fit_curve()` estimates every model parameter freely from the data.
Sometimes you know more about the system than the data alone can tell the
model, for example that a readout cannot exceed a physical maximum. In these
cases you can place bounds on individual parameters.

To illustrate, we use the built-in `iris` dataset. Petal width and petal length
aren't a growth curve, but their relationship has a saturating shape that makes
a convenient example. We first express each measurement as a percentage of its
maximum, so both variables run from 0 to 100.

```{r}
iris_percent <- data.frame(
  width = iris$Petal.Width / max(iris$Petal.Width) * 100,
  length = iris$Petal.Length / max(iris$Petal.Length) * 100
)

ggplot2::ggplot(iris_percent, ggplot2::aes(x = width, y = length)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  theme_dosefitr()
```

## Unconstrained fit

We start by fitting a four-parameter sigmoid with no constraints.

```{r}
iris_model <- fit_curve(
  data = iris_percent,
  x_var = "width",
  y_var = "length",
  curve_options = list(model = "four_param_sigmoid")
)

iris_model$curve$nls_model

plot_model(
  list = iris_model,
  x_var = "width",
  y_var = "length"
)
```

## Bounding a parameter

Bounds are passed through `curve_options` as named lists, `upper_bounds` and
`lower_bounds`, where each name matches a model parameter. Because length is
expressed as a percentage of its maximum, the curve should not plateau above
100. However, we can cap the top at 80.

```{r}
iris_model_bounded <- fit_curve(
  data = iris_percent,
  x_var = "width",
  y_var = "length",
  curve_options = list(
    model = "four_param_sigmoid",
    upper_bounds = list(top = 80)
  )
)

iris_model_bounded$curve$nls_model

plot_model(
  list = iris_model_bounded,
  x_var = "width",
  y_var = "length"
)
```

Comparing the parameter estimates with the unconstrained fit, `top` is now held
at or below 80, and the remaining parameters adjust to compensate.
`lower_bounds` works the same way, for example `lower_bounds = list(bottom = 25)`
to stop the lower plateau falling below 25.

## Combining bounds with outlier handling

Parameter bounds can be combined with the outlier options described earlier.

```{r}
iris_model_bounded_outlier <- fit_curve(
  data = iris_percent,
  x_var = "width",
  y_var = "length",
  curve_options = list(
    model = "four_param_sigmoid",
    upper_bounds = list(top = 80)
  ),
  outlier_options = list(huber = TRUE, rout = TRUE)
)

iris_model_bounded_outlier$curve$nls_model

plot_model(
  list = iris_model_bounded_outlier,
  x_var = "width",
  y_var = "length"
)
```
